title: FULL OUTER JOIN and CROSS JOIN
description: Learn when to keep all rows from both tables with FULL OUTER JOIN, and how CROSS JOIN creates a Cartesian product of every row combination.

data.text: LEFT JOIN keeps all rows from the left table; RIGHT JOIN keeps all from the right. What if you need all rows from *both* tables? That is the job of FULL OUTER JOIN. And what about combining every row with every other row — that is a CROSS JOIN.
FULL OUTER JOIN — all rows from both tables

FULL OUTER JOIN (or just FULL JOIN) returns every row from both tables. Where rows match, the columns are combined. Where they don't, the unmatched side gets NULL. It is the union of LEFT JOIN and RIGHT JOIN.

data.title: FULL OUTER JOIN syntax

data.text: In a project-tracking app, you want to see every project — even those without assigned members — and every member — even those not yet assigned to a project:

data.title: FULL OUTER JOIN of members and projects
data.code:
SELECT m.name  AS member,
       p.title AS project
FROM   pm.members m
FULL OUTER JOIN pm.projects p
    ON p.id = m.project_id
ORDER BY p.title;

data.title: Find gaps on both sides
data.text: Adding WHERE m.id IS NULL OR p.id IS NULL to the FULL OUTER JOIN returns exactly the unmatched rows from both sides — members without projects and projects without members.

data.title: Unmatched rows from both sides
data.code:
SELECT m.name  AS member,
       p.title AS project
FROM   pm.members m
FULL OUTER JOIN pm.projects p
    ON p.id = m.project_id
WHERE  m.id IS NULL
    OR p.id IS NULL;

data.text: A CROSS JOIN produces the Cartesian product of two tables: every row in the first paired with every row in the second. With no ON clause, there is no matching logic. If T1 has n rows and T2 has m rows, the result has n * m rows.

data.title: CROSS JOIN syntax
Combining products with stores
data.code:
SELECT p.product_name, s.store_name, 0 AS quantity
FROM   production.products p
CROSS JOIN sales.stores s
ORDER BY p.product_name, s.store_name;

data.title: CROSS JOIN can be huge
data.text: 1,000 rows crossed with 1,000 rows = 1,000,000 rows. Always ask whether you really need every combination — and consider filtering with WHERE afterward to avoid overwhelming your memory and network.
A practical use: finding missing combinations

CROSS JOIN is useful when you need a complete matrix and then want to find what is missing. For example, list every product-store combination, then LEFT JOIN actual sales onto that to find which combinations have zero sales.

data.title: Find products with no sales in any store
data.code:
SELECT s.store_id,
       p.product_id,
       ISNULL(c.sales, 0) AS sales
FROM   sales.stores s
CROSS JOIN production.products p
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT s.store_id, p.product_id,
           SUM(i.quantity * i.list_price) AS sales
    FROM   sales.orders o
    INNER JOIN sales.order_items i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
    INNER JOIN sales.stores s ON s.store_id = o.store_id
    INNER JOIN production.products p ON p.product_id = i.product_id
    GROUP BY s.store_id, p.product_id
) c ON c.store_id = s.store_id AND c.product_id = p.product_id
WHERE  c.sales IS NULL;

data.title: Quick reference
points: FULL OUTER JOIN keeps all rows from both sides; unmatched columns are NULL
CROSS JOIN pairs every left row with every right row — no ON clause needed
CROSS JOIN row count = rows_in_left * rows_in_right — use carefully
CROSS JOIN + LEFT JOIN is a powerful pattern for finding missing combinations
Prefer LEFT JOIN over RIGHT JOIN for readability; swap the table order if needed
